title: Inverse Gibbs models, identifiability and correlated uncertainty

items.title: Finite exponential Gibbs family for inverse inference
items.statement:
Let $X$ be a finite nonempty set, let $k\in\mathbb N$ with $k\ge1$, let $w:X\to(0,\infty)$ be a positive reference weight, and let $T:X\to\mathbb R^k$. Here $\mathbb R^k$ consists of functions $k\to\mathbb R$, with $k=\{0,\ldots,k-1\}$. On this page use the one-based coordinate labels $v_j:=v(j-1)$ for $1\le j\le k$ and $v\in\mathbb R^k$; in particular $T_j(x):=T(x)(j-1)$. Thus the Euclidean inner product is $\theta\cdot T(x):=\sum_{j=1}^k\theta_jT_j(x)=\sum_{i<k}\theta(i)T(x)(i)$. For $\theta\in\mathbb R^k$, define the partition sum and log-partition function by
$$Z(\theta):=\sum_{x\in X}w(x)e^{\theta\cdot T(x)},\qquad A(\theta):=\log Z(\theta),$$
and define the finite exponential Gibbs family by
$$\pi_\theta(x):=w(x)e^{\theta\cdot T(x)-A(\theta)}\quad(x\in X).$$
All objects here are mathematical; $\theta\cdot T(x)$ is a real number. The representation is called minimal when there is no nonzero $a\in\mathbb R^k$ for which $a\cdot T(x)$ is constant over all $x\in X$.

For a finite set $S\subseteq\mathbb R^k$, its convex hull is the set of sums $\sum_{s\in S}\lambda_s s$ with $\lambda_s\ge0$ and $\sum_{s\in S}\lambda_s=1$. Its affine hull is the set of sums of the same form with real coefficients $\lambda_s$ whose sum is $1$. The relative interior of a convex set is its interior in its affine hull with the Euclidean subspace topology. These definitions will be used for the sufficient-statistic support $T(X)$.

items.title: Supporting direction at a boundary point of a finite full-dimensional polytope
items.statement:
Let $X=\{x_1,\dots,x_m\}$ be finite and nonempty, let $k\ge1$, and let $T:X\to\mathbb R^k$ have full affine hull, meaning that the affine combinations $\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_jT(x_j)$ with $\sum_ja_j=1$ fill $\mathbb R^k$. Define the finite convex hull
$$K:=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{m}\lambda_jT(x_j):\lambda_j\ge0,\ \sum_{j=1}^{m}\lambda_j=1\right\}.$$
If $\mu\in K$ is not an interior point of $K$ in $\mathbb R^k$, then there is a Euclidean unit vector $u\in\mathbb R^k$ such that $u\cdot(T(x)-\mu)\le0$ for every $x\in X$.

items.title: Exact finite-MLE criterion for a minimal finite exponential Gibbs family
items.statement: Use the finite exponential family, minimality, convex hull, affine hull, and relative-interior definitions from the A-page finite-family Definition. Assume the representation is minimal. The sample space is $X^n$ with product mass $\prod_{i=1}^n\pi_\theta(x_i)$, which is the IID sampling model; $n\ge1$. For a realized tuple $x_1,\dots,x_n\in X$, set $\bar T=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nT(x_i)$ and $K=\operatorname{conv}(T(X))$. A finite MLE is a parameter $\hat\theta\in\mathbb R^k$ attaining the maximum of that likelihood. Then a finite MLE exists if and only if $\bar T\in\operatorname{ri}K$, and when it exists it is unique.

items.title: Finite latent Gibbs observation model
items.statement:
Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a nonempty measurable parameter space and let $\vartheta:(\Theta,\mathcal T)\to(\mathbb R^k,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^k))$ be measurable. Let $X$ be the finite state set of the finite exponential Gibbs family from the A-page Definition, evaluated at canonical parameter $\vartheta(\theta)$; write its mass as $\pi_{\vartheta(\theta)}(x)$. A finite latent Gibbs observation model consists of a prior probability measure $\Pi$ on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and a probability kernel $K$ from $(\Theta\times X,\mathcal T\otimes2^X)$ to a nonempty measurable data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, where $2^X$ is the full power-set sigma-algebra on $X$ and $\mathcal T\otimes2^X$ is the product sigma-algebra. The kernel $K((\theta,x),B)$ is the observation law for data event $B$ when parameter $\theta$ and latent configuration $x$ are fixed. Define the marginal sampling kernel
$$Q(\theta,B):=\sum_{x\in X}\pi_{\vartheta(\theta)}(x)K((\theta,x),B)\qquad(B\in\mathcal Y).$$
Thus the latent configuration is summed out before the data likelihood is evaluated.

In a dominated observation model, a specified measure $\nu$ on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ is sigma-finite, meaning that $\mathsf Y$ is a countable union of measurable sets of finite $\nu$-measure. A density is given by a map
$$k:\Theta\times X\times\mathsf Y\to[0,\infty]$$
measurable from $(\Theta\times X\times\mathsf Y,(\mathcal T\otimes2^X)\otimes\mathcal Y)$ to $[0,\infty]$ with its Borel sigma-algebra. Writing its value as $k(y\mid\theta,x)$, for every $(\theta,x)\in\Theta\times X$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$ it satisfies
$$K((\theta,x),B)=\int_B k(y\mid\theta,x)\,\nu(dy),\qquad \int_{\mathsf Y}k(y\mid\theta,x)\,\nu(dy)=1.$$
The marginal data density, or likelihood density at $y$, is then
$$L(\theta,y):=\sum_{x\in X}\pi_{\vartheta(\theta)}(x)k(y\mid\theta,x).$$
The general kernel model does not require a pointwise likelihood density.

items.title: Posterior kernel and dominated formula for a latent Gibbs observation
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let the parameter and data spaces $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ of a finite latent Gibbs observation model both be standard Borel, and let $\Pi$ be its proper prior. Let $J$ be the joint prior-predictive probability determined by $\Pi$ and the marginal sampling kernel $Q$, and let $J_Y$ be its data marginal. There exists a data-indexed probability kernel $y\mapsto\Pi_y$ satisfying
$$J(A\times B)=\int_B\Pi_y(A)\,J_Y(dy)\qquad(A\in\mathcal T,\ B\in\mathcal Y),$$
and any two such posterior kernels agree as probability measures for $J_Y$-almost every $y$.

In the dominated case with data measure $\nu$ and joint likelihood density $L(\theta,y)=\sum_{x\in X}\pi_{\vartheta(\theta)}(x)k(y\mid\theta,x)$ from the Definition, define
$$m(y):=\int_\Theta L(\theta,y)\,\Pi(d\theta).$$
Then $m$ is measurable, $\int_{\mathsf Y}m\,d\nu=1$, and for $\nu$-almost every $y$ with $0<m(y)<\infty$ the posterior has the version
$$\Pi_y(A)=\frac{\int_A L(\theta,y)\,\Pi(d\theta)}{m(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
The prior-predictive law gives zero mass to the set where $m=0$ or $m=\infty$; the conditional identities do not determine pointwise posterior values there.

references.title: Alicia A. Johnson, Miles Q. Ott, and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 2

items.title: Finite-volume Gibbs pseudo-likelihood with fixed boundary
items.statement:
Let $d\ge1$, let $\Lambda$ be a finite nonempty subset of $\mathbb Z^d$, let $S$ be a finite nonempty spin set, let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a nonempty measurable parameter space, and fix a boundary configuration $\eta\in S^{\mathbb Z^d\setminus\Lambda}$. Let $\mathcal C$ be a finite collection of finite subsets $C\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ with $C\cap\Lambda\ne\varnothing$. For each $C\in\mathcal C$, let $\Phi_C:S^C\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be finite-valued and measurable in $\theta$ for each spin assignment. For $\sigma\in S^\Lambda$, let $\bar\sigma$ equal $\sigma$ on $\Lambda$ and $\eta$ outside $\Lambda$, and define the finite-volume energy
$$H_\theta^\eta(\sigma):=\sum_{C\in\mathcal C}\Phi_C(\bar\sigma|_C;\theta).$$
Its normalized Gibbs law is
$$\pi_\theta^\eta(\sigma):=\frac{e^{-H_\theta^\eta(\sigma)}}{\sum_{\tau\in S^\Lambda}e^{-H_\theta^\eta(\tau)}}.$$
For site $i\in\Lambda$, define its finite interaction neighborhood
$$N_i:=\left(\bigcup_{\substack{C\in\mathcal C\\i\in C}} C\right)\setminus\{i\}.$$
For $\sigma\in S^\Lambda$ and $s\in S$, write $\sigma^{i=s}$ for the configuration obtained by replacing only its $i$th spin with $s$. The one-site conditional and finite-volume pseudo-likelihood are
$$q_{i,\theta}^\eta(s\mid\sigma_{\Lambda\setminus\{i\}}):=\frac{e^{-H_\theta^\eta(\sigma^{i=s})}}{\sum_{a\in S}e^{-H_\theta^\eta(\sigma^{i=a})}},\qquad PL_\theta^\eta(\sigma):=\prod_{i\in\Lambda}q_{i,\theta}^\eta(\sigma_i\mid\sigma_{\Lambda\setminus\{i\}}).$$
Every conditional uses the same fixed exterior boundary and is determined by the specified finite neighborhood $N_i$. The product is a finite conditional objective; it is not defined as a probability law on $S^\Lambda$.

references.title: Julian Besag, Statistical Analysis of Non-Lattice Data, The Statistician 24(3) (1975), 179–195
references.locator: §1, printed pp. 179–181, for site-conditional distributions and neighborhoods; §3.3, printed pp. 190–192, especially equation (3.2), for the pseudo-likelihood product and its distinction from the true likelihood.

title: Inverse Gibbs models, identifiability and correlated uncertainty — Examples

items.title: All-plus data have no finite Bernoulli-spin field MLE
items.statement:
Let $X=\{-1,+1\}$, $w(-1)=w(+1)=1$, and $T(\sigma)=\sigma$. For a finite field $h\in\mathbb R$, the Gibbs probabilities are
$$\pi_h(+1)=\frac{e^h}{e^h+e^{-h}},\qquad \pi_h(-1)=\frac{e^{-h}}{e^h+e^{-h}}.$$
For a sample of $n\ge1$ spins all equal to $+1$, the log likelihood is
$$\ell(h)=n\left(h-\log(e^h+e^{-h})\right).$$
It is strictly increasing at every finite $h$, so the likelihood has no finite maximizer. The empirical statistic mean is $1$, a boundary point of $\operatorname{conv}\{-1,+1\}=[-1,1]$.

items.title: Two-spin pseudo-likelihood is not the exact joint posterior input
items.statement: Take $\Lambda=\{1,2\}$, $S=\{-1,+1\}$, and any fixed exterior boundary; the sole interaction set $\{1,2\}$ has no exterior sites, so its energy is independent of that boundary. Use parameter space $\Theta=\{0,1\}$ with its full power-set sigma-algebra, prior mass $1/2$ at each parameter, and the single potential $\Phi_{\{1,2\}}((\sigma_1,\sigma_2);J)=-J\sigma_1\sigma_2$. Use the real exponential $\exp$, put $e:=\exp(1)$, and define $\cosh J:=(\exp(J)+\exp(-J))/2$. For the hypothetical observation $(+1,+1)$, the exact joint likelihood is $\exp(J)/(4\cosh J)$, whereas the product of the two one-site Gibbs conditional probabilities is $[\exp(J)/(2\cosh J)]^2$. By pseudo-posterior I mean the probability vector obtained by multiplying this product by the prior weights and normalizing over $J\in\{0,1\}$. The exact and pseudo-posterior distributions are different.

references.title: Julian Besag, Statistical Analysis of Non-Lattice Data, The Statistician 24(3) (1975), 179–195
references.locator: §3.3, printed p. 190, equation (3.2): the product of site-conditional probabilities is not the true sample likelihood except for independent variables; the two-spin posterior calculation below is local.
